We do not plead for them that it was lost through unavoidable accident. The Shach argues at length in favor of the dissenting authorities, but his words are not sufficient to decide against Tosafot, the Rosh, and the Tur, whose view is supported by the straightforward reading of the Gemara. The opposing camp was forced into many strained explanations, as is well known from the works of the authorities. The Shach's principal argument is: how can we plead for the heirs that the deposit was returned by virtue of a migo that it was lost through unavoidable accident, when we do not plead the claim of unavoidable accident itself for them? This is no argument. According to every view one must explain that when the Gemara says the creditor collects the whole amount, the heirs admitted that no unavoidable accident occurred, or as the Baal HaMaor explains, that if an unavoidable accident had occurred the decedent would certainly have instructed his household concerning it. Yet all agree that if the decedent himself were alive he could claim that he returned it by virtue of the migo that it was lost through unavoidable accident. The same structure can therefore apply according to Tosafot and their school. This is also logically correct. Every case where we charge heirs on a documented loan rests upon the inference: if the debt had been paid, why is the document still in the creditor's possession? Here that inference is absent. We can say that the depositary returned the object and did not insist on retrieving his document because he continually thought: whenever the depositor sues me, I will be believed by a migo that the object was lost through unavoidable accident. The fact that this alternative claim requires a bailee's oath is not enough to make him insist on retrieval of the document. Perhaps he was willing to risk having to take an unnecessary oath and did not regard that concern as sufficient to prevent him from leaving the document outstanding. This is precisely what the Gemara asks in Bava Batra 70 concerning Rav Chisda's rule that a depositary is believed to say "I returned it" by a migo that he could say "it was lost through unavoidable accident." The Gemara asks: does not the latter claim require an oath? In other words, how can a person return the deposit without taking back the document merely because he expects to have the migo of unavoidable accident, when that migo would still force him to swear? Why should he return without his document and expose himself to an oath? The answer is that he is indeed believed only with an oath, but fear of an oath is not enough to make it implausible that he left the document. This is simple. The authorities have discussed it at unnecessary length, and there is no difficulty in the Shach's argument. There is, however, a genuine difficulty for this position. The Gemara says that Rav Chisda's rule, that one who deposited property under a written document is believed to say "I returned it" by a migo of unavoidable accident, is dependent on a tannaitic dispute. A baraita teaches concerning a sh'tar kis issued against orphans that the judges of exile say the holder collects the entire amount, while the judges of Eretz Yisrael say he collects half. The Gemara labors to explain the dispute. Why did it not explain simply as follows? At the initial stage, the dispute appears very broad. According to the view that he collects half, the claim "I returned it" must be sufficiently common that we plead it for heirs. According to the view that he collects all, that claim is not even within the range of ordinary concern. Why not say that the latter holds a claim of return is uncommon and therefore not pleaded for heirs, while the former holds it sufficiently common and therefore pleads it, allowing collection only of half? If the depositary himself were alive and expressly insisted, "I returned it," what difference would it make that the claim is uncommon? According to all opinions he would be believed by his migo. Rav Chisda would then be correct without depending upon the tannaitic dispute. One might answer even according to those who disagree with Tosafot and hold that we do plead uncommon claims for heirs. The dispute could instead be whether an uncommon migo is accepted. The view that the creditor collects the whole amount might hold that the migo from "it was lost through unavoidable accident" is uncommon and an uncommon migo is ineffective, like the view of Rabbi Shimshon of Kinon cited above in the rules of migo. The opposing view could hold either that an uncommon migo is accepted, like those who disagree with Rabbi Shimshon, or that the claim of return itself is also uncommon and therefore can be supported by an equally uncommon migo. But this is not satisfactory if the claim of return is regarded as common because the holder may have retained the document for the scribe's fee. Then there is no migo to an uncommon accident claim according to the first view. The other view could disagree either about uncommon migo or about how common the claim of return is. Yet this entire discussion concerns a sh'tar kis, where the document might indeed be retained for the scribe's fee. With an ordinary deposit, by contrast, all should agree that a return without retrieving the document is uncommon. Why would he leave the document? Precisely because the return claim itself is uncommon, it can be supported by the equally uncommon migo of unavoidable accident. Rav Chisda, who discusses an ordinary deposit, would therefore remain correct according to everyone. The Gemara's presentation as a tannaitic dispute would still be difficult. According to what I wrote above in the rules of migo, however, all agree that "I returned it" is intrinsically an uncommon claim when a document remains outstanding. The reason we nevertheless plead it for heirs is the combination of two possibilities: perhaps the item was lost through unavoidable accident, and if not, perhaps it was returned. The accumulation of two distinct possibilities elevates what would otherwise be an uncommon concern into a sufficiently plausible one for heirs. On this basis the Gemara's structure is explained. It never considered saying that one opinion regards "I returned it" as independently common. Rather, that opinion holds that the combination of possibilities makes the overall defense sufficiently plausible. The view that the creditor collects the entire amount must therefore hold that "I returned it" is not a legally cognizable defense at all in this setting. It is strained to say that the tannaim dispute the bare statistical proposition whether combining two concerns converts an uncommon claim into a common one, since the underlying reasoning is sound. The Gemara can therefore correctly treat Rav Chisda's rule as dependent on their dispute. This also answers the first difficulty according to Tosafot. We cannot say that the view collecting the entire amount merely regards "I returned it" as uncommon and therefore does not plead it for heirs. Everyone agrees it is uncommon standing alone. The only reason to plead it is its combination with the possibility of unavoidable accident. It is not plausible that the tannaim dispute whether two combined concerns have cumulative force. The view that rejects the defense must therefore regard return as legally unavailable in this documented setting, and the dispute genuinely bears upon Rav Chisda's rule. According to this, however, Tosafot's view that we plead "I returned it" for heirs must refer to a case where the decedent had not instructed his household and the heirs do not know that no unavoidable accident occurred. If it is known that no unavoidable accident occurred, the return claim remains alone, and is an uncommon claim not pleaded for heirs. There is then no combination. This requires study, because neither the Tur nor the Shulchan Aruch hints at such a qualification. There is yet another difficulty. What compelled Tosafot to decide that we do not plead unavoidable accident for heirs because it is uncommon? They ask that here Rava rules that the holder of the sh'tar kis collects half upon oath, whereas elsewhere in Shevuot he appears to rule against Rav Chisda that one who deposited under a document is not believed to say "I returned it" unless he has witnesses. The Rashbam, Tosafot, and Riva offer several answers. But initially, before the Gemara had found its later explanation for the opinion that the holder collects the entire amount, it was forced to say that "I returned it" is not pleaded for heirs. Tosafot therefore had to press themselves to say that even unavoidable accident is not pleaded because it is uncommon. Once the Gemara concludes by explaining that the decedent would have instructed his household, however, perhaps everyone agrees that even uncommon claims may be pleaded for heirs. The reason the holder collects the whole amount could simply be that if an unavoidable accident had occurred the decedent would certainly have left instructions, as the Baal HaMaor explicitly writes. He would be even more likely to give instructions concerning an unavoidable accident than concerning an ordinary return, because the depositor would otherwise have no knowledge of what happened. On that basis, Rava could disagree with Rav Chisda entirely. A claim of return in the face of a written document might be legally unavailable according to everyone. The opinion collecting the entire amount would say that even the unavoidable accident claim is not pleaded because the decedent would have instructed his household. The opinion collecting half could hold that death itself prevented him from doing so, and therefore we plead unavoidable accident and allow collection only of half. Rava could then rule like the latter, while still maintaining that if the depositary himself is alive, admits no accident, and says only "I returned it," he is not believed and must prove return by witnesses. That would explain the authorities who rule against Rav Chisda. Accordingly, to defend Tosafot we must explain the earlier stage more carefully. So long as the Gemara assumed according to everyone that death may prevent instruction, it treated as an established principle that if a claim of return is not pleaded for heirs because it is uncommon, then the depositary himself also cannot be believed by such a claim supported by the accident migo. Why? If he truly returned the item, why should its uncommonness matter when he personally asserts it? The answer is that if the depositary could safely rely on a migo of unavoidable accident, that reliance itself explains why he returned the object without retrieving the document. But if he knows that, should he suddenly die, the heirs will not be given the benefit of that defense because it is too uncommon, then it is implausible that he would leave the document in the depositor's hands. He might die unexpectedly without instructing his household, the creditor would collect from the heirs, and strangers would consume his wealth. Why would he create such a danger by returning the property without taking his document? Therefore, unless the law also protects his heirs by pleading the combined possibilities for them, his own claim of return is weakened to the point that the migo cannot explain his conduct. Thus, at the initial stage, the cases are linked. One cannot say that the heirs are denied the uncommon defense but the living depositary is believed by it, because the very fact that his heirs would be exposed makes his conduct of returning without the document unreasonable. Once the Gemara introduces the possibility that a person normally gives instructions to his household, however, the matter changes. A depositary could return the item and rely on the fact that if he dies he will have instructed his household. That can make his own return claim credible even if, in a case where no instruction is found, the heirs receive no such plea. This is the basis of the later distinction. This also explains why Tosafot can infer from the final structure that an uncommon claim is not ordinarily pleaded for heirs. If the Gemara held that even an uncommon claim is freely pleaded, it would not need the special explanation that the decedent would have instructed his household. It could simply distinguish a sh'tar kis from an ordinary deposit by saying that the return of a documented deposit is uncommon, yet is still pleaded for heirs, and Rav Chisda's case would create no difficulty. The fact that the Gemara needs the instruction rationale shows that mere uncommon defenses are not pleaded for heirs. This is precise, and the entire sugya is thereby coherent. The same logic also illuminates the Shach's earlier point concerning repayment within the fixed time. If repayment within the fixed time is so uncommon that we would not plead it for heirs, then even while alive the debtor's claim is weakened. How could he have repaid while leaving the document, relying upon an argument that would fail if he died unexpectedly and the creditor collected from his heirs? This supports the approach explained above.
Or if he died within the time fixed for payment. The Shach, seif katan 7, asks that whether we say a migo against the chazakah that a person does not repay within the fixed time is an unresolved question, as stated above in siman 78. Here the depositary has a migo that he could have claimed an unavoidable accident. Why then should it matter that the matter was still within the fixed time? The Shach answers that perhaps the case concerns heirs. A claim of repayment within the fixed time is uncommon, and we do not plead an uncommon claim for heirs. He notes, however, that the wording does not imply this. See his lengthy discussion. In truth, I find no implication in the Tur one way or the other. Yet the Mechaber's words indicate otherwise. Concerning the general rule that we plead for heirs that the deposit was lost through unavoidable accident, he cites two opinions whether an uncommon claim is pleaded for heirs. The ruling here that within the fixed time we do not plead that the item was returned is stated without qualification according to all opinions. This demonstrates that the reason is not merely that such repayment is uncommon. Likewise above in siman 71, seif 22, the Mechaber cites first the opinion that where a creditor granted the debtor general credibility, we plead even for heirs that repayment occurred within the fixed time, despite its uncommon nature. Indeed, it is not clear to me that a matter contrary to the chazakah that a person does not repay within the fixed time should be classified as "uncommon" for purposes of what we plead for heirs. The category of a matter so uncommon that it is not pleaded for heirs requires something genuinely rare. The Rosh writes in Perek Shnei Dayanei Gezeirot that a claim of forgery is uncommon, yet we nevertheless plead forgery for heirs. One must therefore say that only something thoroughly uncommon is excluded. It is known that a majority is stronger than a chazakah. If anything contrary to a chazakah were called uncommon, then all the more so something contrary to a majority would be uncommon. Yet in Ketubot 16 the Gemara asks: since most women marry as virgins, what does it matter if witnesses do not come? Tosafot write that this question is according to Rav, who follows the majority even in monetary matters. Why did the Gemara not instead ask even according to Shmuel from the Mishnah of "she became widowed," since how can we plead for the heirs a claim contrary to the majority that most women marry as virgins? It follows that even a claim contrary to a majority is not automatically treated as an uncommon claim for heirs. All the more so one contrary merely to a chazakah. The Shach's difficulty can instead be answered in several ways. First, the question whether a migo is effective against the chazakah that a person does not repay within the fixed time remains unresolved. According to many authorities, including the Mechaber, whenever a Talmudic monetary question remains unresolved, if the claimant has seized the disputed property, even in the presence of witnesses, it is not removed from him. See above in the laws and rules of kim li and seizure. If so, why would a depositary return property within the fixed time and leave the document in the creditor's possession? One might answer that he relies upon the migo that he could say the property was lost through unavoidable accident, and therefore is not careful to retrieve the document, as the Gemara in Bava Batra explains. But how can he safely rely upon that? The creditor might later seize property from him in the presence of witnesses and claim kim li that no migo is effective against the chazakah. The debtor would then have no means to recover it. Why would he leave the document in the creditor's hands when at any moment the creditor could openly seize his property and no one could rescue it from him? Thus the chazakah expressed by "what is your document doing in my hand?" becomes especially strong, and the claim of return is not believed. A second answer is that the migo of "it was lost through unavoidable accident" is itself a weak migo, because such accidents are uncommon. According to many authorities, a migo based on an uncommon claim is not accepted. See above in the rules of migo. Whether a migo is effective against the chazakah of no repayment within the fixed time is itself unresolved. Here, therefore, there are two weaknesses: the migo runs against a chazakah, and the alternative claim supporting it is uncommon. When both defects are present, no one accepts the migo. Thus within the fixed time, where we would need both a migo against the chazakah and an uncommon alternative claim of unavoidable accident, the migo is ineffective. The Rosh's words in the first chapter of Ketubot point this way. He asks concerning one who says, "I found an open entrance," and is believed because of the chazakah that a person does not toil over a wedding feast and then deliberately destroy it. Why is the woman not believed that she was a virgin by a migo that she could have said, "I was violated after betrothal"? The Rosh answers that she does not wish to disqualify herself from the priesthood. He then asks that the husband should have a migo from claiming that she had been previously violated, and answers that such a claim is uncommon. This implies that the Rosh regards "I was violated after betrothal" as a sufficiently common claim, for otherwise he could have answered the first question simply by saying that the alternative claim is uncommon. Apparently, once according to his account she was in fact not a virgin, a violation during the marriage relationship is not treated as extraordinarily uncommon. Yet the Gemara on 12 says that according to Rabban Gamliel she is believed when she says, "I was violated after betrothal," by a migo that she could have said she was injured by a piece of wood after betrothal, even though that alternative is uncommon. See what I wrote above in the rules of migo, siman 46. The Tur and Rosh can therefore hold that a migo based on an uncommon claim alone may sometimes be effective. But where it is also opposed by an independent chazakah, the two defects combine, and such a migo is not accepted. The same applies here: it is both an uncommon alternative claim and a migo against the chazakah of no repayment within the fixed time. According to this, however, Tosafot's question in Bava Batra 5b, s.v. mi, loses much of its force. Tosafot ask from the rule that one who deposits with a written document must return the deposit in the presence of witnesses, even though he has a migo that he could claim unavoidable accident. This would show that a migo is not effective against a document, and all the more so not against the chazakah that one does not repay within the fixed time, which is stronger than a document because a document still requires an oath when collecting from heirs, whereas a claim within the fixed time does not. According to what was stated, there is no proof. In the case of a documented deposit, there is the chazakah created by the document, "what is your document doing in my hand?," together with the uncommon migo of unavoidable accident. When both are present, no migo is accepted. In the case under discussion in Bava Batra, however, there is only a migo against the chazakah of no repayment within the fixed time, and the Gemara therefore remains uncertain. Tosafot's proof would not follow. There is yet a third answer. The principle "what is your document doing in my hand?" is indeed a chazakah, as Tosafot write, but it is a relatively weak one, and therefore a migo can overcome it, especially because the possessor also has the chazakah of possession of money. When another chazakah is added to it, however, the two chazakot together constitute a strong chazakah. Against a strong chazakah all agree that a migo is ineffective, as Tosafot write in Ketubot 9. See the rules of migo above. Here there is both the chazakah created by the document and the chazakah that a person does not repay within the fixed time. Against two chazakot no migo is accepted. At first glance this too seems to conflict with Tosafot's question in Bava Batra. Tosafot had already written that a document is like witnesses except that the chazakah is weakened by the possibility that the creditor retained it for reimbursement of the scribe's fee. With a written deposit, however, the depositor gives the fee, as Tosafot in Bava Batra and Shevuot explain. The depositary therefore cannot say that the document was retained for the scribe's fee. The document should then be equivalent to actual witnesses, and it would be obvious that no migo is effective against it, because a migo is never effective against witnesses. How could Tosafot infer anything from that case about the weaker chazakah of no repayment within the fixed time? It must be that Tosafot's question follows the Rashbam's explanation on Bava Batra 70. Rami bar Chama asks how the Torah's oath of bailees can ever arise, a powerful question according to the Rashbam, who finds no solution until the Gemara establishes a deposit evidenced by a document that must be returned in the presence of witnesses. Tosafot's later answer, that since the alternative claim itself requires an oath there is no migo to exempt from another oath, is plainly not accepted by the Rashbam. One must say that he holds that the oath on a claim of return is not a Torah oath. Otherwise the question how the Torah's oath of bailees can arise would already be resolved. The Rashbam's words later indeed show that according to Rami bar Chama there is no solution except a documented deposit for which return must be proved by witnesses. If so, one can ask how the oath of a borrower who says the animal died through ordinary use can ever arise. The borrower has a migo that he returned it. The only solution is where the loan was documented and return requires witnesses. But in the case of a borrower, who receives all the benefit, the borrower must surely pay the scribe's fee. Thus the lender may have retained the document for that fee. Even with that weak chazakah, the migo is rejected. Tosafot's question is therefore valid. One might ask why the Gemara could not establish the case as a loan of an object for a fixed period, where the borrower claims within that period that it died through use. Then he cannot claim that he already returned it. At first glance this supports the Shach's question that even within the fixed time the unresolved migo question remains. Yet this is not decisive. Abaye and Rava, who state the relevant discussion, hold that people sometimes repay within the fixed time. Rami bar Chama could follow Reish Lakish, who disagrees, so Tosafot could still ask according to him. Moreover, even Abaye and Rava might agree that their reason, "a person sometimes repays within the time so that the creditor will not trouble him later," applies only to a loan of money, which is spent and may not be readily available at maturity. It does not apply to a borrowed object that must itself be returned. What concern of later pressure is there when the very object remains present? Thus the question from a borrower remains strong. In my novellae I have already written that independently there is little difficulty from a borrower. If the lender retained the document for the scribe's fee, then when he sues for the borrowed object he will surely also claim the scribe's fee owed to him. The borrower who says, "I returned the object," must explain the fee. If he says he repaid the fee too, his claim is a migo against witnesses, because he admits paying everything yet left the document in the lender's hands, which is evidence that his claim is false. If he admits he did not repay the fee and says this is why the lender retained the document, then the lender claims the object plus a small monetary amount and the borrower admits the small amount. This is a partial admission requiring a Torah oath. There is therefore no migo to exempt him from the Torah oath of a bailee, because even the alternative claim of return would itself require a Torah oath. The document itself cannot be treated as immediate payment for the small sum. Even according to those who regard a pledged object as immediate payment, the erased or written parchment is plainly worth less than the scribe's fee, and both the scribe's labor and the value of the document have been consumed. There is no full immediate payment. It therefore seems that Tosafot understood the phrase "he retained it for the scribe's fee" not literally as the only reason. They used one possible explanation. The broader point is simply that retention of a document is not equivalent to witnesses, because there may be some other reason the document was not returned, such as that it was lost and the holder is still searching for it. This point requires some study. In any event, there are three sound approaches to explain the Tur and Shulchan Aruch, and the Shach's difficulty is not decisive.
Either he believed in a business owner and so on, I wrote above C. D.M. from Burma, the author, even with no loyalty to me. And we have to do so with our loyalty to Him, but not to shine forth, and to the exaltation of Hashem’s judgment, and to give him allegiance to Hashem’s mercy, and to Hashem’s mercy, and to Hashem’s mercy, and to Hashem’s mercy, he would not have been able to lose him A fleet to claim that no lithami was wrong, therefore, because he was not a sign of an eye, and in the oath he was adopted by D. D. D. D. D. even gave him loyalty to P.M., committed to swearing against orphans, but he did not need a oath, but did not lose money:
That an unavoidable accident occurred. If the custodian was only an unpaid bailee, the Knesset HaGedolah questions whether we plead for the heirs that the deposit may have been stolen or lost. He writes that many authorities regard theft and loss as common enough that such a plea is made for heirs according to all views. This, however, creates a difficulty in the Gemara's challenge to Rav Chisda from the opinion that the creditor collects the entire amount of a business investment document. Perhaps that authority holds only that the bailee lacks a migo from unavoidable accident, because a business custodian is a paid bailee and an unavoidable accident is uncommon, so an uncommon migo is not recognized. Rav Chisda, by contrast, stated his rule regarding an ordinary deposit. An unpaid bailee can plead theft or loss, which are common claims, and therefore has a normal migo that all would recognize. If so, the Gemara would have no question. It therefore appears that no distinction should be made. This is also implied by the unqualified language of all the poskim. All the more so according to the Rambam, who holds that with an iska the half treated as a deposit imposes only the responsibility of an unpaid bailee, yet even there we do not plead for the heirs theft or loss, but only repayment.
Or exchanged property. This ruling requires study. The Rif, Rosh, and Rambam mention only merchandise that came directly from the original investment, meaning that the deceased received money and purchased the identified goods with those very funds. Such goods are unquestionably treated as the investor's property and may be collected without an oath. If the original merchandise was later exchanged, however, perhaps the deceased first returned the investor's property and then acquired the present goods with his own funds. Maharam says explicitly in the responsa printed with Mishneh Torah, Sefer Kinyan, din 11, that if the merchandise changed form and was exchanged for other goods, we plead for the heirs that the original property may have been returned, based on the migo that an unavoidable accident could have occurred. The Tur in Yoreh Deah siman 176 nevertheless includes exchanged property, and from there the Mechaber took the present ruling. The issue therefore rests on an actual dispute among authorities and requires study.

urim_vetumim_urim.he:
שטר עסקא ענין עסקא הוא דפלגא הוא פקדון ביד המקבל ולכך הרווח ממנו שייך לנותן ומפקיד ופלגא השני הוא מלוה ובזה הרווח למקבל ולא לנותן דלא יהיה רבית והוא מקבל שכר עמלו בפלגא פקדון ולכך הוא ש"ש על הך פלגא וחייב בגניבה ואבידה ופטור מאונסין משא"כ בחצי השני חייב כמו שארי הלואה ועיין בי"ד הלכות רבית כללי עסקא יותר באריכות: ולכך על הך פלגא נשבע ונוטל כדין הבא ליפרע מנכסי יתומים משא"כ באידך פלגא אלו היה המקבל חי היה נאמן בש"ח דהחזיר במגו דהיה טוען נאנסו והיה נאמן בשבועה אף בזו נאמן בשבועה א"כ במותו טענין ליתומים ולא אמרינן דהא ה"ל מחויב שבועה וכשאין יכול לישבע משלם דלגבי יורשים לא אמרינן כן רק כשהוא חי וה"ל למידע ולישבע:
ודוקא אם אין להם אפטרופסים כו' כן כתבו הר"ן והרא"ש כתובות דף ק"ט ע"ב דטען אפטרופס ואמר אביי שפיר קטען דאר"י וכו' והקשו למה המתין אביי עד שטען אפטרופוס ותי' זה דאין לדיין לטעון עד שיטעון אפטרופוס אבל תוס' שם ד"ה אמר וכו' כתבו דאביי לא היה זכור מתחלה דין דר"י אבל אם היה זכור היה טוען וא"כ לא ס"ל הך דינא ומ"מ נראה דראה רמ"א לסמוך אדברי הר"ן והרא"ש:
ואין עליהם שבועה כי לפטור אין צריך שבועה שלא פקדנו אבא רק מקבלים בחרם שלא צוה להם אביהן דלא פרע:
או שמת ת"ז וכו' דחזקה אין אדם פורע ת"ז והש"ך השיג ע"ז דהא יש לו מגו דנאנסו והך איבעיא לא אפשטא אי אמרינן מגו במקום חזקה כזו. ולכן דעתו דלכך לא מהימן משום דהוי מילתא דל"ש ולא טענין ליתמי הא אלו חי וטען כן נאמן אפילו בת"ז במגו וכן להך מ"ד דס"ל דטענין נאנסו ליתומים אף דהוי מילתא דל"ש ה"ה בת"ז טענין החזרתי במגו וע"ת שבררתי כדעת הטור ומחבר דל"א מגו כזו ולכ"ע לא טענינן ליתמי וגם אם הוא חי וטען כן אינו נאמן ע"ש:
או שהאמין לבעל עסקא דתו לא מצי הוא לטעון החזרתי אף ליתומים לא טענינן כן ומ"מ צריך שבועה דלענין שבועה י"ל לגבי לוה האמינו ונגד יורשי הלוה לא האמינו משא"כ לענין ממון ועיין תומים ועיין לעיל סימן ע"א דיש מחלוקת בפוסקים אי בעינן דוקא נאמנות כבי תרי אבל נגד נאמנות סתם מהני מגו ולהך דיעה צ"ל כאן דהימנו כבי תרי ועיין תומים לעיל סימן ע"א:
אין טוענים להם שנאנסו דהוי מילתא דלא שכיח ולא טענין ליתמי ועיין תומים שכתבתי די"ל אם ידוע שלא נאנסה אף החזרתי אין טוענים ליתומים וע"ש באריכות בישוב הקושיא שיש לדעה זו ועיין לעיל בכללי מגו בישוב קושיא דהא ה"ל מגו לא שכיח:
שנאנסו ואם הוא שומר חנם אם לטעון להם גניבה ואבידה העליתי דג"כ לא שכיח ולא טענינן ליתמי ועיין תומים. אבל החזרתי טוענין אף בפקדון במגו דנאנסו אף דלא שייך דזייר שטרא אפשיטי דספרא ועיין תומים ולקמן סימן רצ"ו:
או חליפיו וכו' עיין תומים דבחליפין של עסקא שלקח במעות סחורה והחליף הסחורה בסחורה אחרת צ"ע אם נוטל הב"ח ולא טענין ליתומים החזרתי ע"ש:
ואם יש רווח וכו' היינו דהיה עסקא על זמן ומת המקבל תוך זמן ובטלה העסקא וה"א דאין ליתומים רווח דרווחא משתעבד עד כלות זמן עסקא קמ"ל כיון דיסתלק ויתבטל העסקא יש להם חלקם ברווח סמ"ע:
urim_vetumim_urim.en:
An iska note. An iska is structured so that half the capital is a deposit in the recipient's possession. The profit from that half therefore belongs to the investor. The other half is a loan, and its profit belongs to the recipient rather than the investor, to avoid interest. The recipient receives compensation for his work with the deposit half and therefore has the status of a paid custodian for that half, liable for theft and loss but exempt from unavoidable accidents. With respect to the loan half, he is liable as with any loan. See Yoreh Deah, laws of interest, for the full rules of iska. Accordingly, concerning the loan half the investor swears and collects like any creditor collecting from heirs. Concerning the deposit half, if the recipient were alive he could claim, 'I returned it,' through a migo that he could have claimed that it was lost through an unavoidable accident, and would be believed with an oath. Therefore, after his death we make the corresponding claim for the heirs. We do not say that he was one who was obligated to swear and, being unable to swear, must pay. That principle is not applied to heirs in such a case, where the deceased is no longer alive to know and swear.
Specifically if they have no guardians, etc. Ran and Rosh write this in Kesubos 109b. There the guardian first raised the claim, and Abaye said that he had argued well because Rabbi Yochanan said so. They ask why Abaye waited until the guardian raised it, and answer that a judge does not plead for the heirs until a guardian has been appointed to argue for them. Tosafos there instead write that Abaye had initially forgotten Rabbi Yochanan's ruling, implying that had he remembered it he would have raised the claim himself. Tosafos therefore do not accept this rule. Nevertheless, Rama evidently relied on Ran and Rosh.
And they have no oath. To be exempt, heirs need not take the heirs' oath that their father did not instruct them. They merely accept a cherem that their father did not tell them that the debt had been paid.
Or he died within the term, etc. There is a presumption that a person does not pay before the due date. Shach objects that the recipient has a migo that the deposit was lost through unavoidable accident, and the question whether such a migo is effective against this presumption is unresolved. Shach therefore explains that the reason is instead that a claim of return in such circumstances is unusual, and we do not plead an unusual claim for heirs. According to him, if the recipient himself were alive he would be believed even within the term through the migo, and according to the opinion that we plead unavoidable accident for heirs even though it is unusual, we would likewise plead return within the term. See Tumim. I clarified that Tur and the Mechaber are correct: such a migo is not accepted, and all agree that we do not plead it for heirs. Even if the recipient is alive and makes that claim, he is not believed. See there.
Or he gave the investor credibility. Then the recipient himself could no longer claim that he returned the funds, and therefore we do not make that claim for his heirs. Nevertheless, the investor must still swear, because the credibility clause may have been intended only against the borrower himself, not against his heirs. See Tumim. Above in siman 71 there is a dispute whether an ordinary credibility clause is sufficient against a migo, or whether the creditor must be believed like two witnesses. According to the latter view, the present case must involve credibility like two witnesses. See Tumim above in siman 71.
We do not plead for them that it was lost through accident. That is an uncommon event, and we do not plead uncommon claims for heirs. See Tumim. I wrote that if it is known that no accident occurred, perhaps we likewise do not plead 'I returned it.' See there at length for the resolution of the difficulty on this opinion, and see the general rules of migo concerning an uncommon migo.
That it was lost through accident. If the recipient was an unpaid custodian, whether we plead theft or loss for the heirs, I concluded that these too are uncommon and are not pleaded. See Tumim. But we do plead 'I returned it,' even concerning a deposit, through a migo that he could have claimed unavoidable accident, even though the concept that one preserves a receipt for incidental writing expenses does not apply in the same way. See Tumim and below in siman 296.
Or its substitutes, etc. See Tumim. Where business capital was used to purchase merchandise, and that merchandise was exchanged for other merchandise, it requires study whether the creditor takes the substituted merchandise without allowing the heirs to claim that the original capital was returned. See there.
And if there is profit, etc. This means that the iska was for a fixed term and the recipient died during that term, terminating the arrangement. One might have thought that the heirs receive no profit because profit was assigned only through the end of the iska term. The ruling teaches that since the arrangement terminates early, the heirs receive their proportionate share of the profit. See Sema.

mechaber.he: מת המלוה ובאים יורשיו לתבוע השטר מהלוה והוא אומר פרעתי לאביהם והם אומרים לא ידענו אומרים לו זיל שלים ואם אומר השבעו לי אם יש בשטר שהאמין את המלוה ואת יורשיו עליו גובין בלא שבועה ואם לא האמין אותם עליו ישבעו בנקיטת חפץ שלא צוה להם אביהם על ידי אחר ושלא אמר להם בפיו ושלא מצאו שובר בין שטרותיו ששטר זה פרוע שאם מצאו שובר עליו הי' בחזקת פרוע והוא שנמצא השטר בין שטרות קרועים כמו שנתבאר (סי' ס"ה) ויכללו בכלל השבועה שלא אמר להם אביהם שהיה לו שטר פרוע בין שטרותיו אפי' היה היורש קטן המוטל בעריסה כשמת מורישו ה"ז נשבע כשיגדיל ונוטל ומיהו אין זה צריך לישבע אלא שלא מצאתי אבל שלא פקדנו אבא לא דלאו בר צוואה היה:
mechaber.en: If the lender died and his heirs come to collect the document from the borrower, while the borrower says, 'I paid their father,' and they say, 'We do not know,' he is told, 'Go and pay.' If he says, 'Swear to me,' then if the document grants credibility to the lender and his heirs, they collect without an oath. If it does not grant them credibility, they swear while holding a sacred object that their father did not instruct them through another person, did not tell them orally, and that they found no receipt among his documents stating that this note was paid. Had they found such a receipt, it would be presumed paid, provided the note was found among torn documents, as explained in siman 65. Their oath also includes that their father did not tell them that he had placed a paid note among his documents. Even if an heir was a minor lying in a cradle when the ancestor died, he swears and collects upon reaching adulthood. Such an heir need swear only, 'I did not find a receipt.' He need not swear, 'Our father did not instruct us,' because he was not capable of receiving instructions.

baer_hetev.he:
אמר. וכתב הרא"ש פ"ק דב"מ שאם יש להם עד א' שאמר האב דשטר זה אינו פרוע גובין בלא שבועה ע"ש. ש"ך:
מצאתי. ולפ"ז אפשר דה"ה בנולד אחר מיתת האב נמי צריך לישבע וכ"כ הטור והה"מ בשם ר"מ ועיין בס' א"א דף פ"ד שכתב דלהרמב"ם לא קי"ל כר"י וא"צ לישבע ודבריו נראין עכ"ל הש"ך וכתב הסמ"ע דגם שלא צוה להן אביהן ע"י אחר א"צ לישבע דכל שאין ראוין לצוות להן בפיו מחמת קטנותן אין דרכו לצוות להן לפי שעה ע"י אחר אלא היה כותב הדבר לזכרון או היה משים הדבר בפי אפוטרופסים:
baer_hetev.en:
Said. The Rosh writes in the first chapter of Bava Metzia that if the heirs have one witness who heard the father say that this promissory note had not been paid, they collect without an oath. Shach.
I found. According to this, it is possible that even a child born after the father's death must take an oath, and the Tur and Maggid Mishneh write so in the name of Maharam. See Imrei Noam, page 84, which writes that according to the Rambam we do not rule like Ri and no oath is necessary. The Shach says that this appears correct. The Sema writes that even where the father did not communicate the matter to them through another person, they need not swear. When the children are too young for him to instruct directly, a person does not ordinarily send them a temporary message through someone else; rather, he records the matter for later or entrusts it to their guardians.

beer_hagolah.he:
שם ס"מ וכן כתב הרמב"ם ריש פ' י"ז
שם סעיף ט' בשם אביו הרא"ש בתשו' כלל ע"א סי' ז'
כך כ' גם הרמב"ם שם וכתב ה"ה זו היא שבועות היורשים המוזכרת במשנה פרק כל הנשבעין וכו' דף מ"ה ע"א ומ"ש שם השתא אבוהון שקיל בלא שבועה וכו' הני מילי בדלא טעין אשתבע לי וכו' אבל בדטעין לישתבע לי כיון דאי הוה טעין הכי לאבוהון היה נשבע וכו' אינהו נמי נשבעין שבועת היורשין וכ"כ רבינו האי והרי"ף ז"ל בתשו' וכן עיקר והא דלא העמידו המשנה בדבאין ליפרע מן הלוה עצמו ובטוען ישבע תירץ כמ"ש בסוף סעיף א' בשם הב"י וע"ש
משנה שם
סעיף י"ח עיין במ"ש שם
שם כ"כ בסה"ת שער י"ד
ל' הרמב"ם שם בפי"ז דין ב' וכ' ה"ה מתוך דברי רבינו נראה שפוסק כת"ק דר' יוחנן בן ברוקא שם במשנה דע"כ לא נחלקו אלא בנולד לאחר מיתת אביהן דלת"ק לא בעי שבועה אבל בקטן אפילו תנא קמא מודה
טור ס"י כך כ' בה"ת בשער י"ד
beer_hagolah.en:
There is a book, and it is written by the Rambam
The name of Hashem’s name is the name of His father, the Holy One, in the name of the Holy One
Rambam likewise writes this there. The Maggid Mishneh explains that this is the oath of heirs mentioned in the Mishnah, chapter Kol HaNishba'in, Shevuot 45a. As for the Gemara's statement there, 'Now their father would have collected without an oath,' etc., that applies where the borrower did not claim, 'Swear to me.' But where he did make such a claim, since the father would have been required to swear, his heirs too must take the oath of heirs. Rav Hai and Rif likewise write this in responsa, and this is the primary view. As for why the Mishnah was not established as a case where the heirs collect from the borrower himself and he claims that they should swear, the Maggid Mishneh answers as explained at the end of seif 1 in the name of Beit Yosef. See there.
Change there
Seif 18. See what is written there.
This is the name of the gate
The language of Rambam there, chapter 17, law 2. The Maggid Mishneh writes that from Rambam's words it appears that he rules like the first Tanna who disputes Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka in the Mishnah there. Their dispute concerns only one who was born after the father's death, where according to the first Tanna no oath is required, but with a minor even the first Tanna agrees that an oath is required.
This is what Hashem says in the door

beur_hagra.he:
מת כו' אומרים לו כו'. כמ"ש בשבועות מ"ז א' אבוהון כו':
אם יש כו'. כתובות פ"ו ב':
ואם לא כו'. עבה"ג ס"ק ג' וכ"מ שם מדקא' אבוהון כו' הא במקום שאביהן נשבע אף הן נשבעין והא דלא אוקים בגמ' כה"ג משום דמתני' לא איירי בהכי:
בנק"ח. כמו שבועת המשנה כנ"ל מדקא' מאי בין זה לפוגם שטרו:
שלא צוה כו' ושלא אמר כו'. כן פי' בסה"ת שם ח"ב בשם י"מ מ"ש שלא פקדנו ולא אמר לנו כו'.
והוא שנמצא כו'. ספ"ק דב"מ:
ויכללו בכלל כו'. כמ"ש בסוף ב"ב קע"ג א' האומר שטר בין כו' ומה שלא נזכר במתני' משום שנכלל במ"ש שלא אמר לנו אבא כו' וז"ש ויכללו כו':
אפי' היה כו'. עבה"ג אבל בשם הרמ"ה כ' דהלכה כריב"ב דליכא מאן דפליג וכ"כ בסה"ת שם ח"ו:
ומיהו כו'. ערש"י שם ד"ה ה"ז נשבע כו' ועסמ"ע:
beur_hagra.en:
He died... they say to him... As stated in Shevuos 47a concerning the oath the father would have had to take.
If there is... Kesubos 86b.
And if not... See Beer HaGolah. The Gemara's wording indicates that where their father could have sworn, they too may swear. It did not establish the Mishnah in such a case because the Mishnah concerns a different scenario.
While holding a sacred object. Like a Mishnah-level oath, as above, since the Gemara compares it to one who impairs his document.
That he did not instruct... and did not tell... Baal HaTerumos cites an explanation of the phrases "he did not instruct us" and "he did not tell us" in this manner.
And provided that it was found... End of the first chapter of Bava Metzia.
And they shall include in the general wording... As stated at the end of Bava Basra 173a regarding one who says "a document among..." The Mishnah does not mention it separately because it is included in the phrase that their father never told them.... Hence the text says they should include it in their oath.
Even if it was... See Beer HaGolah. In the name of the Ramah it is written that the halachah follows Rabbi Yehudah ben Beseira, since no one expressly disputes him. Baal HaTerumos writes similarly.
Nevertheless... See Rashi there and Sema.

chelkat_mechokek.he: הנותן מתנה לאשתו או לבנותיו. כלומר שנתן לאשתו או לבתו שיטלו חלק כא' מן הזכרים ורוצה להערים וליתן במתנה אח"כ רוב נכסיו לבניו כדי שלא יגיע לאשה רק חלק קטן בין הבנים וכן אם נתן לבנותיו חלק בין הזכרים יערים ויתן לאשתו מתנה מרובה כדי שלא יגיע להם רק חלק קטן בירושה ועיין בתשובת מהרי"ל סי' צ"ב:
chelkat_mechokek.en: Give a gift to his wife or daughters. That is to say that he gave his wife or daughter a portion of the males and wants to make a gift later to his sons so that he would not reach the woman only a small part of the boys, and if he had given his daughters a part of the forest males and given his wife a great gift so that they would not only have a small part of his inheritance and see the answer from the IDF

meirat_einayim.he:
גובין בלא שבועה. לשון הטור שהרי אין שבועה מוטלת על היורשים כ"א שלא פקדנו ומשבועה זו פטרם במ"ש הנאמנות למלוה וליורשיו דהא לא היה עליהן שום שבועה אלא זו:
בין שטרות הקרועים כו'. כיון דאיכא ריעותא להשטר מורה שנפרע המלוה מהלוה ולא היה השט"ח בידו להחזירו לו וכתב עליו שובר והא דנמצא השובר ביד המלוה ולא ביד הלוה י"ל שמא הלו' האמין למלוה והפקיד השובר בידו עד שיחפש השט"ח וכשלא ימצאהו יקח מידו השובר אבל אי לא מצא השט"ח בין הקרועים אמרי' דהשט"ח בחזקתו והשובר הכין המלו' באם יבא הלוה לפרוע לו פתאום ולא יהיה בידו השט"ח להחזירו וגם לא יהיה לו אז פנאי לכתוב לו שובר שיהיה שובר זה מוכן בידו לתנו לו ואף אם נמצא השט"ח בין הקרועין ולא מצאו שובר ביד אביהם המלוה היו גובין ג"כ בהשטר והיינו אומרים דנזדמן כך שבא השט"ח בין הקרועין ועדיין לא נפרע וכל זה נתבאר בסי' ס"ה בטור ובדברי המחבר שם סי"ח ע"ש:
שהי' לו שטר פרוע כו'. דין זה נתבאר בטור ובדברי המחבר לעיל ס"ס ס"ה סכ"ג ע"ש:
אבל שלא פקדנו אבא לא. וגם שלא צוה להן אביהן ע"י אחר אין עליהן לישבע דכל שאין ראויין לצוות להם בפיו מחמת קטנותן אין דרכו לצוות להן לפי שעה ע"י אחר אלא היה כותב הדבר לזכרון או היה משים הדבר בפי אפוטרופסים ועיין בב"י:
meirat_einayim.en:
They collect without an oath. The Tur explains that the only oath that could have rested upon the heirs was the oath that their father had not instructed them that the debt was paid. The credibility clause granted by the borrower to the lender and his heirs exempts them from that oath, because no other oath was applicable to them.
Among the torn documents, etc. Because the debt instrument itself has a defect indicating possible payment. Perhaps the lender was paid but did not have the note available to return to the borrower, so he wrote a receipt instead. Although the receipt is found in the lender's possession rather than the borrower's, perhaps the borrower trusted the lender and left the receipt with him until the lender could search for the original note, intending to take the receipt if the note could not be found. If the note is not found among the torn documents, however, the document retains its presumption of validity. We then say that the lender prepared the receipt in advance in case the borrower suddenly came to pay when the lender did not have the note available to return and would lack time to write a receipt. Even if the note itself was found among the torn papers, if no receipt was found in the lender's possession the heirs would still collect on the note, because we would say that it happened to be placed there and had not yet been paid. All this is explained in siman 65:18.
He had a wild bar. This sentence is explained in the column and in the words of the above S. S.C.:
But they do not swear that our father did not instruct us. Nor must they swear that their father did not instruct them through another person. Since, because of their minority, they were not fit to receive such instructions directly from him, it is not his ordinary practice to give them a temporary message through another person. Rather, he would write the matter down as a record or entrust it to guardians. See the Beit Yosef.

rabbi_akiva_eiger.he: [שו"ע] ודהיתה ת"ז צריך שיקבל. נ"ב ובמבש"ט וכתב בו זמן אם מקבלים עידי קיום בעוד שהיתומים קטנים עמ"ש הסמ"ע וש"ך לעיל סי' ע"ח:
rabbi_akiva_eiger.en: [Shulchan Aruch] And if the due date had passed, he must accept. Note: Regarding a documented loan bearing a date, whether testimony authenticating the document may be received while the heirs are minors, see what the Sema and Shach write above in siman 78.

siftei_kohen.he:
ישבעו כו'. עיין באשר"י רפ"ק דמציעא כתב שאם יש להם ע"א שאמ' האב דשטר זה אינו פרוע גובין בלא שבועה ע"ש:
בנקיטת חפץ. אדסמיך ליה קאי כשאומר להן הלוה השבעו לי דאל"כ אין צריך לישבע כדמוכח בש"ס פ' כל הנשבעין ופרק הכותב ובטור ובכל הפוסקים מיהו אם פוגמים השטר או עד אחד מעיד שהוא פרוע או שבאו ליפרע מנכסים משועבדים צריכין לישבע בכל ענין כ"כ ר"י נ"ט ח"ב ע"ש ודוק והב"י מביאו בסוף סעיף ח' ועיין בר' ירוחם עצמו ותראה שכוונתו כמ"ש ועמש"ל ר"ס פ"ד:
והוא שנמצא כו'. כלומר הא דהשטר בחזקת פרוע היינו שנמצא בין השטרות קרועי' לפיכך צריכים היורשים לישבע אף בסתם דשמא היה שם שובר והיה השטר מונח בין הקרועים וכן משמע מלשון הרב המ' ר"פ י"ז מה' מלוה ודלא כספר לח"מ ס"פ ט"ז מה' מלוה שנרא' מדבריו שהבין דאין היורשים צריכין לישבע שבועה זו אא"כ ידעו שהשטר היה מונח בין הקרועים ולכן כתב שהרמב"ם סתם הדברים יותר מדאי וה"ל לבאר שנמצא בין השטרות קרועים כמו שביאר פרק ט"ז מה' מלוה ולפי מ"ש לא היה צריך לבאר כאן כלום וק"ל עוד כתב הלחם משנה שם דגם בפרק כ"ד מהלכות מלוה שכתב הרמב"ם וכן אם נמצא לאחד בין שטרותיו שובר ששטר של יוסף בן שמעון פרוע כו' סתם הרמב"ם והל"ל דמיירי שנמצא בין השטרות קרועים כדאוקמי' בסוף פרק קמא דמציעא כו' ולא דק בזה דהרמב"ם בפ' כ"ד מה' מלו' מיירי להדי' בשובר שאצל הלוה ויוסף בן שמעון הם המלוים וכמו שכתב הרמב"ם להדיא שטרות שניהן פרועין וכאוקימתא דאביי בפרק גט פשוט ד' רע"ג ע"א עיין שם וכמו שכתב הרי"ף והרא"ש פרק ג"פ והך דסוף פרק קמא דמציעא היינו לאוקימתא דר' ירמיה וכמ"ש התו' פרק גט פשוט שם וזה ברור:
אלא שלא מצאתי. ולפ"ז אפשר דה"ה בקטן שנולד אחר מיתת אב נמי צריך לישבע וכ"כ הטור והרב המ' בשם ר"מ ועיין בספר א"א דף פ"ד ע"ד שכתב דלהרמב"ם לא קי"ל כר"י ואין צריך לישבע ודבריו נראין ודוק ועיין ב"י וסמ"ע:
siftei_kohen.en:
They shall swear, etc. See the Rosh at the beginning of the first chapter of Bava Metzia, who writes that if they have one witness who heard the father say that this document has not been paid, they collect without an oath; see there.
While holding a sacred object. This refers to the immediately preceding case, where the borrower says to them, 'Swear to me.' Otherwise they need not swear, as is evident from the Gemara in Kol HaNishba'in and in HaKotev, and from the Tur and all the authorities. However, if they impair the document by admitting partial payment, or one witness testifies that it was paid, or they come to collect from encumbered property, they must swear in every case. So writes Rabbeinu Yerucham, Netiv 9, part 2; see there carefully. The Beit Yosef cites him at the end of seif 8. Examine Rabbeinu Yerucham himself and you will see that his intent is as I have written. See also what I wrote above at the beginning of siman 84.
Provided that it was found, etc. Meaning, the reason the document is presumed paid is that it was found among torn documents. Therefore the heirs must swear even without a specific demand, for perhaps there had been a receipt and for that reason the document was placed among the torn documents. This is also implied by the wording of the Maggid Mishneh at the beginning of chapter 17 of Hilchot Malveh, unlike Lechem Mishneh at the end of chapter 16 of Hilchot Malveh, who appears to understand that the heirs need swear this oath only if they knew that the document had been placed among the torn documents. He therefore wrote that the Rambam stated the matter too briefly and should have explained that it was found among torn documents, as he explained in chapter 16 of Hilchot Malveh. According to what I have written, however, there was no need for him to explain anything here. Lechem Mishneh further wrote there that in chapter 24 of Hilchot Malveh as well, where the Rambam writes that if among a person's documents a receipt is found stating that the document of Yosef ben Shimon was paid, the Rambam should have specified that it was found among torn documents, as the Gemara establishes at the end of the first chapter of Bava Metzia. He was not precise in this, for in chapter 24 the Rambam expressly discusses a receipt found with the borrower, while the two persons named Yosef ben Shimon are the lenders, as the Rambam explicitly writes that both of their documents are paid. This follows Abaye's explanation in Bava Batra 173a, as the Rif and Rosh write in Gittin Peshutin. The passage at the end of the first chapter of Bava Metzia follows the explanation of Rabbi Yirmeyah, as Tosafos write in Gittin Peshutin there. This is clear.
Rather, that I did not find. According to this, it is possible that the same applies to a minor born after his father's death, who must also swear. So write the Tur and the Maggid Mishneh in the name of Rabbi Meir. See Sefer Even HaEzel, folio 84d, who writes that according to the Rambam we do not rule like Rabbi Yochanan and no oath is required. His words appear correct. Examine this carefully, and see the Beit Yosef and Sema.

urim_vetumim_urim.he:
והוא שנמצא שטר וכו' דעל נמצא שובר לחוד י"ל כתב שובר אם יבא הלוה לפרוע יהיה השובר מוכן ולא יהיה עיכוב בדבר ועל מציאת בין שטרות הקרועים ג"כ י"ל אתרמי אבל בדאיכא תרתי לריעותא חיישינן ופשוט דאין אנו צריכין לידע בבירור שנמצא שטר בין שטרות הקרועים רק אנו חוששים דלמא מצאו יתומים שובר והשטר בין שטרות הקרועים ומכחישים אותו ולכך אנו מטילים שבועה עליהם להודות אמת ואם נודע לנו בבירור שלא נמצא אין עליהם שבועה כלל ממציאת שובר דאף דנמצא לא מהני לחוד ש"ך:
אלא שלא מצאתי וכו' אבל א"צ לישבע שלא צוה ע"י אחרים דאין דרך לצוות ע"י אחרים רק מניח הדבר בכתב למשמרת לבניו וא"כ אין להם רק שבועה זו שלא נמצא כתב סמ"ע ודוחק ויותר נראה דע"י מי צוה בפני קרובים או ע"א אין הקטן והבן מחויב להאמין לגרוע כח השטר ולא מפיהם חי וע"י שני עדים כשרים קלא אית להו והיה בלי ספק באים לב"ד והעידו ולכך אין כאן חשש:
שלא מצאתי ואם הוא נולד לאחר מיתת אביו איכא מחלוקת בין הרמב"ם והטור והר"ם דהרמב' אינו מצריכו שבועה והטור והר"ם פסקו דצריך שבועה כמו קטן בחיי אביו והמחבר סתם הדברים כרמב"ם וצריך טעם בסברא מ"ש דהיה בן יום אחד כשמת אביו דצריך שבועה ומ"ש דנולד תיכף אח"כ וצריך לומר קטן לא פלוג עבדי רבנן בין קטן בר דעת לאינו בר דעת משא"כ בנולד אח"כ לא שייך לא פלוג. ועוד דכיון דמת אביו ולא יודע אם יהיה לו זרע קיימא מסתמא מצוה עסקיו לפני עדים או ב"ד והיה ליה קלא:
urim_vetumim_urim.en:
Provided that the note was found, etc. If only a receipt is found, one can say that the lender prepared it in advance so that if the borrower came to pay there would be no delay in producing a receipt. If only the note is found among torn notes, one can say that this happened accidentally. But where both defects are present, we are concerned. It is not necessary to know with certainty that the note was actually found among the torn notes. We are concerned that perhaps the heirs found both a receipt and the note among torn notes and are concealing that fact, and therefore we impose an oath requiring them to tell the truth. If we know for certain that the note was not found among torn notes, no oath is imposed merely because a receipt was found, for a receipt alone is insufficient. This is Shach's explanation.
Only that I did not find, etc. He need not swear that his father did not communicate the matter through others. Sema explains that a person does not ordinarily transmit such instructions through others, but would leave a written memorandum for his children. Therefore the heir need swear only that he found no such writing. This is strained. It appears more correct that if the father gave instructions before relatives or one witness, the minor son is not bound to accept their statement to weaken the note, because legal matters are established through living testimony and not merely their report to him. If the instruction was before two valid witnesses, it would become publicly known and they would presumably come to beit din and testify. Therefore there is no independent concern.
That I did not find. If the heir was born only after his father's death, Rambam and Tur together with Maharam disagree. Rambam does not require him to swear, while Tur and Maharam require the same oath as for a child who was alive during the father's lifetime. The Mechaber's general wording follows Rambam. The distinction requires explanation. Why should a child who was one day old when his father died have to swear, while one born immediately afterward does not? One can answer that concerning a child already alive, the Sages did not distinguish between a child capable of understanding and an infant incapable of understanding. A child not yet born at the time of death falls outside that uniform enactment. Additionally, when a man dies not knowing whether he will leave surviving offspring, he presumably arranges his affairs before witnesses or beit din, and the matter would become known.

mechaber.he: אם יש לקטן אפוטרופוס שמינהו אביו ומבקש חובותיו של קטן צריך לישבע שלא צוהו אבי היתומים ושלא מצא בין שטרותיו ששטר זה פרוע ואם מינוהו ב"ד אינו צריך לישבע אלא שלא מצא בין שטרותיו ששטר זה פרוע:
mechaber.en: If a minor has a guardian who has appointed his father and asks for the debts of a small man, the father of orphans and who has not found between his notes that this trend is wild, and if he is identified in the D, he should not swear unless he has found a wild one:

baer_hetev.he: לישבע. ל' הטור ואין חוששין שמא ימנע מלהיות אפוטרופא כמ"ש ר"ס ר"צ שלא ימנע בשביל זה שמצוה הוא עושה בשבועה זו כדי שלא יפסידו היתומים את חובם עכ"ל ור"ל דלא אמרו דפטורים משבועה בעבור חששא זו אלא כשיצטרכו לישבע שלא לקחו ממעות היתומים ומשום שרע בעיניהן שחושדין אותם. סמ"ע:
baer_hetev.en: Swearing. The column is not afraid that he will refrain from being a judge as a R.C. who will not be prevented for the fact that he does in this oath so that the orphans will not lose their bonds and that they will not be told that they will not be harmed by the orphans and because they are evil in their eyes. A:

beer_hagolah.he: שם סי"א בשם הראב"ד בתשו' כ"כ בסה"ת שער י"ד
beer_hagolah.en: There, seif 11, in the name of Raavad in a responsum. So writes Ba'al HaTerumot in Gate 14.

beur_hagra.he:
אם יש כו'. כמ"ש אפי' שומר נשבע כו' ול"ד למ"ש מנהו אבי היתומים לא ישבע כי מצוה קעביד כו' ע"ש ח"ו:
ואם מינוהו כו'. כנ"ל ס"ה:
beur_hagra.en:
If there is... As stated that even a guardian takes an oath. This differs from a guardian appointed by the father of the orphans, who may be exempt because he performs a mitzvah without personal benefit.
And if they appointed him... As above in seif 5.

meirat_einayim.he:
צריך לישבע שלא ציווהו אבי היתומים ל' הטור ואין חוששין לומר אם יצטרך לישבע שמא ימנע מלהיות אפטרופס (וכמ"ש הטור והמחבר לקמן ר"ס ר"ץ) שלא ימנע בשביל זה שמצוה הוא עושה בשבועה זו כדי שלא יפסידו היתומים את חובם עכ"ל ור"ל דלא אמרו שפטורים משבועה מכח החששא הנ"ל אלא כשיצטרכו לישבע שלא לקחו ממעות היתומים ומשום שרע בעיניהם שחושדין אותם:
א"צ לישבע. הטעם שודאי אביהם לא ציווהו שהרי אביהן לא מנהו לאפטרופס:
meirat_einayim.en:
It is necessary to swear that my father had not commanded the Tortoise and that he would not be afraid to say if he would have to swear that he would not refrain from being apocalypse (and that he would not lose his debt, and that he would not deny that he was not afraid of the orphans
A to swear. Their father did not say that their father did not give birth to his father

netivot_hamishpat_beurim.he: אם יש לקטן אפוטרופוס. בתומים הקשה דמה ענין לשבועת אפטרופס הא אפטרופס נאמן מטעם עדות כמבואר בסי' ר"צ סעיף י"ב בהג"ה. ולק"מ דודאי שם איירי באפוטרופוס שאינו נו"נ בנכסי יתומים רק באפוטרופוס שנתמנ' לטעון בנכסי יתומים כמ"ש בס' אגודת אזוב דאפטרופס הנו"נ בנכסי יתומים והלוה טוען שפרע להאפוטרופס והאפטרופס מכחיש אין לך נוגע גדול מזה דהא אם יודה לדברי הלוה יצטרך לשלם להיתומים אלא ע"כ באפטרופס שלא נתמנה רק לטעון בנכסי יתומים וכמ"ש בס' א"א הנ"ל משא"כ הכא מיירי באפטרופס הנו"נ כנכסי יתומים וממון יתומים תח"י דאפי' להיתומים הי' צריך לישבע אולי נטל ממון היתומים לעצמו רק משום דחיישי חז"ל לדילמא מימנע והכא כשנשבע נגד הלו' דלא שייך חששא דמימנע כמ"ש הסמ"ע ודאי דחשיב כבע"ד ממש דצריך שבוע' כשבא לגבות דחשדינן ליה דאף שאבי יתומים ציוה שהוא פרוע מ"מ תובע השטר בשביל עצמו ורוצ' לגבות ומשקר בשביל מלוה ישינה שיש לו עליו לכך צריך לישבע כנ"ל ברור:
netivot_hamishpat_beurim.en: If the minor has a guardian. Tumim asks what relevance the guardian's oath has, since a guardian is believed as a witness, as explained in siman 290, seif 12, in the gloss. There is no difficulty. There, the case certainly concerns a guardian who does not conduct transactions with the orphans' property, but was appointed only to litigate concerning their property, as explained in Agudat Ezov. If a guardian who actually conducts transactions with the orphans' property is alleged by the borrower to have received repayment and the guardian denies it, there could be no more interested witness than he, because if he admitted the borrower's claim he would have to reimburse the orphans. The cited ruling must therefore concern a guardian appointed only to litigate. Here, by contrast, the case concerns a guardian who conducts transactions with the orphans' property and holds their money. Even toward the orphans he would ordinarily need to swear, lest he have taken some of their money for himself, but the Sages exempted him because they feared people would refrain from accepting guardianship. Here, when he swears against the borrower, that concern does not apply, as the Sema explains. He is then treated like an actual litigant who must swear when coming to collect. We suspect that even if the orphans' father told him the debt was paid, he might nevertheless sue on the note for his own benefit and falsely seek collection because of some old loan he believes is owed to him. He must therefore swear. This is clear.

netivot_hamishpat_hidushim.he: לקטן אפוטרופס ) (וע"ב כאן מיירי אפוטרופס נו"נ בנכסי יתומים מש"ה אין עליו דין עד וחייב לישבע ובסי' ר"צ סי"ב מיירי שאינו נו"נ בנכסיהם רק שהעמידוהו לטעון בנכסי יתומים לכך יש עליו דין עד:
netivot_hamishpat_hidushim.en: To the small of Apostolics, he has no law until he is sworn to swear, and he is not allowed to be charged with the property of orphans

pitchei_teshuva.he: צריך לישבע. ע' בתומים שהק' הא מבואר לעיל סי' ל"ז ס"ח ולקמן סי' ר"צ סי"ב דאפוטרופס כשר להעיד והרי הוא כשאר עדים ואם כן מה טיבו של שבועה זו הא ה"ל עד א' מסייעו ופוטר משבועה ובפרט בנשבע ונוטל כזה דשורת הדין ליטול בלא שבוע' כו' והאריך בישוב קושיא זו ע"ש ובנה"מ כתב ליישב זה באופן אחר ע"ש גם בת' חוט השני סי' ו' ז' האריך בזה וע' בת' שבו"י חו"ב סי' קע"א שכתב בפשיטות דכאן מיירי בענין שהאפטרופוס הוא פסול לעדות שהוא קרוב וכה"ג לכן הצריכו לישבע משא"כ אם הוא כשר לעדות פשוט הוא שא"צ לישבע כמו כל עד דעלמא ובתשובת חוט השני סי' ו' ז' לא הרגיש בכל זה עכ"ל. ומהאי טעמא פסק שם בעובדא שאפטרופוס של יתמי שמינה אותו אביהם תבע לראובן שמצא כתוב בפנקס שמעון שחייב לו ראובן על משכנו' אלו סך מאה זהובים וראובן טוען שפרע לו בחייו נ' ולא נשאר חייב לו רק חמשי' ומסיק לדינא שצריך ראובן לשלם כפי הכתוב בפנקס ואין לו שום שבועה על היתומים ולא על האפוטרופוס כיון שהוא טוען שלא צוה המוריש כלום ע"ש ועמ"ש לעיל סי' ע"ב הל"ה סקכ"ט:
pitchei_teshuva.en: He must swear. Tumim asks that an appointed guardian is generally qualified to testify, as stated above in siman 37, seif 8, and below in siman 290, seif 12. If so, why is an oath required here? The guardian should be like any other single witness who supports the claimant and exempts him from an oath, especially where the claimant is one who by strict law would take without an oath and the oath is only an added requirement. Tumim gives an extended resolution, and Netivot HaMishpat offers a different answer. Responsa Chut HaShani, simanim 6 and 7, also discusses the issue at length. Shevut Yaakov, volume 2, siman 171, writes simply that the present case must concern a guardian who is disqualified from testimony, such as a relative. Therefore the claimant must swear. If the guardian is qualified as a witness, no oath is required, just as with any other witness. On that basis he ruled in a case where a father-appointed guardian for orphans sued Reuven after finding in the deceased Shimon's ledger that Reuven owed one hundred gold coins on specified pledges. Reuven claimed that he had paid fifty during Shimon's lifetime and owed only fifty. Shevut Yaakov concluded that Reuven must pay according to the ledger entry and has no oath to impose either upon the orphans or upon the guardian, because the guardian claims that the deceased gave him no contrary instruction. See also above, siman 72, seif 35, seif katan 29.

rabbi_akiva_eiger.he: [שו"ע] אין מקבלין עדות ע"ק ואפי' בפניו. נ"ב ואפי' יש שם יורשים גדולים ג"כ ונתקבל העדות בשביל הגדולים לא מהני לגבי הקטנים הר"ם אלשיך ז"ל בשו"ת סי' קכ"ז:
rabbi_akiva_eiger.en: There is no evidence in the face. N.B. and D.A. have great heirs there, and the testimony is received for the great ones not from me regarding the young peoples of the USSR in the USSR:

siftei_kohen.he: צריך לישבע כו'. ע"ל סימן ר"צ בסמ"ע סקל"ד ועמ"ש שם ועיין לעיל סי' ע"ב ס"ק ק"א ומ"ש שם:
siftei_kohen.en: He must swear, etc. See below siman 290 in the Sema, seif katan 34, and what I wrote there. See also above siman 72, seif katan 101, and what I wrote there.

urim_vetumim_tumim.he: אם יש לקטן אפוטרופס וכו' דין זה צ"ע מה טיבו של שבועה זו דהא מבואר לעיל סי' כ"ז ס"א ולקמן סי' ר"צ סי"ב דאפטרופוס הרי כשר להעיד והרי הוא כשאר עדים וא"כ מה טיבו של שבועה הא ה"ל עד אחד ופוטר משבועה דקי"ל ע"א מסייע פוטר מן השבועה. ובפרט בנשבע ונוטל הזה דשורת הדין ליטול בלי שבועה וכמש"ל בסימן פ"ז. ובאמת מרא דהאי שמעתא הוא הראב"ד ז"ל בתשובה כמ"ש הבעה"ת שער י"ד והטור וכפי מ"ש המ"מ פרק כ' מהלכות מכירה לא ס"ל דע"א המסייע פוטר משבועה אך לא לבד דאין זה מעלה ארוכה לטור והמחבר דס"ל דעד מסייע פוטר אף גם בממ"נ אם לא ס"ל דפטור מ"מ אפטרופס בגדר העד הוא ואלו היו שנים היו נאמנים לדברי הכל וא"כ מה יועיל מה שישבע או דנאמן בלי שבועה או דשבועתו אינו מועיל ומגרע גרע דעד המשתבע אין עדותו מועיל כלום כדקי"ל בפרק המקדש ועכצ"ל דאינו בגדר עדות רק ה"ל כבעל דבר ולכר צריך שבועה ומועיל שבועתו וזהו דלא כמ"ש בסי' ל"ז ור"צ דה"ל עדות ולקמן סי' ר"צ ס"ב בהג"ה הביא רמ"א דברי המרדכי בהדיא דאם טוען פרעתי לאפוטרופס מעות של יתומים והאפטרופס מכחישו אם ידוע שהוא מעות של יתומים נאמן האפטרופס וא"צ שבוע' וא"כ הקושי' יותר חזקה דאנו מאמינים לו שלא פרעו ולא נאמין לו שלא פקדיהו אבי היתומים. והדבר נלמוד במכ"ש וצ"ע ויש ליישב ולחלק בדוחק כי אמרינן אפטרופס מעיד והוי כעד היינו שהגדיל היתום והוא תובע והנתבע משיב פרעתי כבר ליתום בזו אמרינן דתו לא הוה אפטרופס בע"ד והוי כעד לכל מילי אבל בעוד היתום קטן ואפטרופס הוא התובע א"כ אף הוא נעשה כבעל דבר וא"י להעיד כי הוא בע"ד וכל דין יתום עליו וצריך לישבע כמו היתום עצמו ודוק. אך כל זה צ"ע כי מקורו של הדין הזה אין לו שרש כי הראב"ד יליף לי' מהך דקתני שומר ואשתו של שומר נשבעי' ונוטלים ושם ליכא שטר כלל ושורת הדין דע"י אמירת הללו לא יהיה נוטל כלל רק חז"ל תקנו מכח התקנה של נגזל וא"כ די דיהיו נוטלי' בשבוע' וכי ס"ד דנוציא ממון עפ"י אמירה גריד' ואף זו דיטלו בשבוע' מכח התקנה. משא"כ כאן דיש כאן שטר מעליא ולהפסת דעת תקנו חז"ל שבועה ואיך נימא לפסול לאפטרופס מעדותו ומכ"ש בשיש שני אפטרופסי' דלהך סברא דה"ל בעלי דינים ה"ה בשנים ואם בשני' א"צ ה"ה בא' דלענין פיטור שבועה אח' דינו כשנים ודוק. ונראה דכל זה מיירי דיש לאפטרופס מגו דאי בעי קלת' אבל אי לית ליה מגו מהכ"ת יהיה כח ביד אפטרופס לגרוע כח יתום וכי מפיו אנו חיי' ולאו כל כמיניה ואפשר דאף הראב"ד לא קאמר אלא כשבא הוא לגבות בו וא"כ איך יגבה אם יודע דהדין עם הלוה אבל באמת אין קורעין השטר ויהיה מונח עד שיגדלו יתומים והוא נדון כע"א מעיד על שטר שפרוע:
urim_vetumim_tumim.en: If the minor has an administrator, etc. This ruling requires study. What is the basis for requiring this oath? It is explicit above in siman 37, seif 1, and below in siman 290, seif 12, that an administrator is qualified to testify and is treated like any other witness. If so, the administrator is a single witness who supports the claimant, and we hold that a supporting single witness exempts from an oath. This should be especially true with an oath imposed on one who collects, where the strict law would allow collection without the oath, as explained above in siman 87. The source of this ruling is the Raavad in a responsum, as cited by the Baal HaTerumot, shaar 14, and the Tur. According to the Maggid Mishneh in Hilkhot Mekhirah, chapter 20, the Raavad does not hold that a supporting single witness exempts from an oath. But that does not resolve the ruling for the Tur and the Mechaber, who do hold that a supporting witness exempts. More fundamentally, even according to the Raavad, an administrator is still in the category of a witness. If there were two administrators they would be believed by everyone. What then can be achieved by having a single administrator swear? Either he is believed as a witness without an oath, or his oath does not transform him into competent testimony. Indeed, a witness who himself takes an oath is not thereby strengthened as a witness, as we hold in the chapter HaMekadesh. We would have to say that in this setting he is not treated as a witness at all, but as a litigant, so an oath is both required and effective. But that directly conflicts with simanim 37 and 290, where an administrator is treated as a witness. Below in siman 290, seif 2, the Rama cites Mordechai explicitly that if a debtor says he paid money belonging to orphans to their administrator and the administrator denies it, where it is known that the money belonged to the orphans the administrator is believed without an oath. If we believe him that he was not paid, all the more should we believe him concerning whether the father instructed the heirs about payment. The difficulty is substantial. One can answer, though somewhat narrowly, that an administrator is treated as a witness only after the orphan reaches majority and brings his own claim. At that stage the administrator is no longer a party to the litigation and may testify like any other witness. While the orphan is still a minor and the administrator himself prosecutes the claim, the administrator functions as the litigating representative and is treated like the orphan for procedural purposes. He then cannot simultaneously serve as an independent witness, and must take the same oath the orphan would have been required to take. Even this requires study, because the source in the Raavad is itself questionable. He derives the rule from the case where a guardian and the guardian's wife swear and collect, but there no debt instrument exists at all. Strict law would not allow collection merely on their statements. The Sages created a special remedy analogous to the enactment for one who was robbed, and it is therefore understandable that they permit collection only with an oath. Here, by contrast, there is a valid debt instrument and the oath is merely a rabbinic safeguard to satisfy the defendant. Why should that safeguard disqualify an administrator from acting as a supporting witness? All the more so where there are two administrators. If the theory is that they are litigants, both would be litigants, but surely two independent qualified administrators should not be weaker than two witnesses. If two exempt from an oath, one supporting witness should likewise exempt where the law recognizes a supporting witness. The better limitation may be that the ruling applies only where the administrator has a migo because he could have destroyed the document. If he has no such migo, by what authority can an administrator weaken the minor's document? We do not live by his admission, and he has no right to harm the minor. Perhaps even the Raavad meant only that when the administrator himself comes to collect while knowing that the claim is not valid, he may not do so without the required oath. The document itself should not be torn, however, but left until the orphans reach majority. At most the administrator is then a single witness testifying that the document was paid.

urim_vetumim_urim.he:
אם יש לקטן אפטרופוס כו' עיין תומים דהעליתי דאם השטר מונח עד שיגדלו היתומים דאז הוא האפטרופוס הנ"ל כעד אחד ופוטר משבועה ומכ"ש אם אפטרופסים הם שנים רק כאן מיירי שהם תובעים בקטנותם וא"כ ה"ל כבע"ד ולכך צריכי שבועה ולפ"ז אפילו הם אפטרופסים שנים וע"ש:
שלא צוהו אבי וכו' ואם אומר שצוה אם השטר בידו דיכול לשורפו ולגונזו נאמן ואם לאו אינו נאמן ואפשר דבקטנותו הוא א"י לתובעו אבל מונח השטר עד שיגדיל ואז ה"ל כע"א מעיד על שטר שהוא פרוע ועיין תומים מ"ש בזה כי כל הדין צ"ע ע"ש:

meirat_einayim.en:
He is not faithful but on his part. P. and the others swear by oath of grace and do not have a faithful man to lose to others in his glory:
There is an opinion that says, etc. The Tur writes that the holder is not believed merely by virtue of a migo that he could have burned the document, except in the case of a true third party with whom both sides deposited it. The reason is that even such a third party is not believed initially because he presently has a migo to burn or conceal it. Rather, he is believed because both parties trusted him from the outset and did not suspect him of burning or hiding it. Since they initially entrusted him, he is believed in all he says concerning it. This reasoning does not apply to ordinary partners or brothers where a debt instrument belonging to the estate comes out from under the hand of only one of them. In the Perishah and at the beginning of siman 56 I explained the language of the Gemara proving this. The ruling in siman 93:14, where a note in Shimon's name against Levi belongs to the partnership of Shimon and Reuven and Shimon says Levi paid, so that Levi is discharged by Shimon's admission, is different. There the document itself was written in Shimon's name. Even though it expressly states that the money belongs to the partnership, since it is in Shimon's hands and bears his name, he is believed to discharge Levi, while Shimon must then pay Reuven his half. Here the document was written in the father's name and was publicly established as the father's document. It was not in this particular heir's power to return or cancel it. Examine this carefully.

netivot_hamishpat_beurim.he: א"נ אלא על חלקו עסמ"ע ס"ק ך"ט עד משא"כ כאן שהשט"ח נכתב ע"ש אביהן והוחזק השטר לרבים בשם אביו וכו'. אין לפרש בדברי הסמ"ע דמיירי שהוחזק בב"ד קודם שאמר פרוע דבזה לא הי' חולק הדיע' ראשונ' דהא מגו למפרע לכ"ע לא אמרינן אלא ודאי דמיירי שאמר פרוע תיכף כשהוציא השטר ונרא' דכוונת הסמ"ע הוא דכבר כתבתי לעיל בסי' צ"ו בביאורים ס"ק י"ח דטעם הרא"ש הוא דלא אמרי' מגו רק בבע"ד או בשליש שהוא כבע"ד אבל מי שיש בידו משל אחר אינו נאמן במה שהוא בידו לקלקל אותו דרשות הנפקד הוא כרשות המפקיד והוי כמגו להוציא וזהו ג"כ כוונת הסמ"ע דבשותפין שנכתב על שמו והרי הימני' שהרי יכול לגבות כל השטר בעצמו ועסמ"ע סי' נ"ו ס"ק ז' דבפקדון שייך ג"ב הימני' מש"ה הוי בבע"ד ונאמן במגו משא"כ בנכתב ע"ש אביו ומוחזק שהוא של אביו ואין אח אחד יכול לגבות כל השטר כמבואר בסי' ע"ז סעיף ט' ע"ש בהג"ה וגם לא בא לידו בפקדון מאחיו ולא שייך ביה הימני' כלל מ"ה אינו נאמן אפי' יש לו מגו ועוד נרא' לענ"ד לחלק דעיקר הטעם דלא מהימן במנו דאי בעי קלתי' דהוי במגו מקום חזקה כמ"ש הש"ך בסי' מ"ז ס"ק ו' ע"ש וע"ל בחידושי' סי' ס"ב ובבאורי' ס"ק ט' ע"ש שחילקתי דבדבר שיכול לו' שלי הוא ואומר של אחר וליכא חשש קנוניא מהני מגו במקום חזקה ודוקא בדבר דאיכא חשש קנוניא לא מהני מגו. ולפ"ז א"ש דבסי' צ"ג ל"מ אם לא כתוב בו שהוא מממון השותפות ודאי דהי' יכול לומר שלי הוא אלא אפי' אם כתב בו שהוא ממון השותפות מ"מ כיון דיכול לגבות כל השטר הרי הלוה נתחייב נגדו בכל המעות ולא יכול לומר לאו בע"ד דידי את ממילא שטר כזה נקנה במסיר' בלא כתיב' ועיין בסי' ס"ו מ"ש בביאורי' ומהימן לומר לקוח כשיש לו מגו או שלי הוא ולפנחיא כתבתי או שלא להשביע לדעת הסמ"ע בסי' ס' ס"ק ך"ח מש"ה כשאמר פרוע מהימן במגו משא"כ בהשטר שנזכר שם אביו שא"י לתבוע בו רק חלקו כמבואר בסי' ע"ז סעיף ט' בהג"ה וממילא צריך כומ"ס ולא מהימן לומר שלי הוא ואיכא חשש קנוניא לא מהני מגו:
netivot_hamishpat_beurim.en: Alternatively, only as to his own share. See Sema, seif katan 29, through his statement that here the promissory note was written in their father's name and publicly established as belonging to their father. The Sema cannot mean that the note had already been established in beit din before the heir said it was paid, because then the first opinion would not disagree. A migo arising only retroactively is ineffective according to all views. Rather, the case is that he declared it paid immediately when producing the note. The Sema's intent appears to follow what I wrote above in siman 96, Biurim, seif katan 18, that the Rosh's reason is that migo is said only regarding a litigant, or a third party custodian who is comparable to a litigant. One who merely holds another's property is not believed, even with a migo, to damage that property. The bailee's possession is considered the depositor's possession, and this is like using a migo to extract property. This is also the Sema's intent. With partners, where the note was written in one partner's name, the other partner trusted him, for the named partner can collect the entire note himself. See Sema, siman 56, seif katan 7, that the concept of trust also applies to a deposit. He is therefore treated as a litigant and is believed through a migo. Here, however, the note was written in the father's name and is known to belong to him. One brother cannot collect the entire note, as explained in siman 77, seif 9, in the gloss, nor did the note come into his hands as a deposit from his brothers. There is therefore no basis for saying they trusted him, and he is not believed even with a migo. Another distinction also appears to me. The principal reason he is not believed through the migo that he could have burned the note is that this is a migo against a chazakah, as the Shach writes in siman 47, seif katan 6. In Chiddushim to siman 62 and Biurim, seif katan 9, I distinguished that where a person could claim, It is mine, but instead says it belongs to another, and there is no concern for collusion, a migo can work against a chazakah. It is only where there is concern for collusion that a migo is ineffective. Accordingly, the distinction is clear. In siman 93, certainly where the note does not state that it is partnership money, he could claim it is entirely his. Even if it states that it is partnership money, since he can collect the entire note, the borrower is liable toward him for the entire amount and cannot say, You are not my litigant. Such a note can therefore be acquired by transfer without a written assignment, as I explained in siman 66, Biurim, and he is believed to claim it was purchased when he has a migo, or that it is his, or, according to the Sema in siman 60, seif katan 28, that he wrote it merely for appearance or so as not to appear wealthy. Therefore, when he says it was paid, he is believed through the migo. Here, however, the note names his father and he can sue upon it only for his own share, as explained in siman 77, seif 9, in the gloss. It therefore requires both writing and transfer, and he is not believed to say, It is mine. Since there is concern for collusion, his migo is ineffective.

siftei_kohen.en: And there are those who say to me that I will see him and his words, and he will see him and his words:

urim_vetumim_tumim.he:
